title: The future destruction of the Achaean wall
greek: τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν (teichos Achaiōn); οὐδὲ θεοῖσι δόσαν κλειτὰς ἑκατόμβας (oude theoisi dosan kleitas hekatombas)
short: The narrator looks beyond the end of the war: after Troy falls, Poseidon and Apollo will turn the rivers of Ida on the Greek wall and wipe it out.
body: The wall and trench were built in one day in Book 7 (433-41), without the hecatombs owed to the gods (12.6). Poseidon complained that its fame would eclipse the wall he and Apollo built for Laomedon, and Zeus allowed him to destroy it once the Greeks had sailed (7.446-63). Here the narrator tells that story in advance, the most extended look forward to the fall of Troy in the whole poem: Achilles' wrath will end, Hector will die, the city will be sacked in the tenth year. The passage answers a practical question, why no trace of the wall could be seen at Troy. Aristotle's dry comment, preserved by Strabo, is that the poet who invented the wall also made it vanish. Leaf treats the wall as a late addition to the story. Modern critics read the passage more positively: Ruth Scodel relates it to Near Eastern flood myths that end an age of heroes, and James Porter explores what it says about poetic making and unmaking.

title: 'The race of half-divine men' (hēmitheoi)
greek: ἡμιθέων γένος ἀνδρῶν (hēmitheōn genos andrōn)
short: The only time Homer calls the heroes 'demigods': a word that belongs to Hesiod's myth of the ages, in which the heroes are a vanished race.
body: Hēmitheoi, 'half-gods', occurs only here in Homer. Monro calls it the only trace in Homer of the idea that the men who fought at Troy were a distinct kind from ordinary mortals; Leaf says it is 'totally inconsistent' with Homer's usual picture, in which the heroes, though often of divine descent and stronger than men of the poet's day, are simply men. The word belongs to Hesiod's myth of the five ages (Works and Days 156-73), where the fourth race is 'the godlike race of hero-men, who are called demigods', destroyed at Thebes and Troy, some of them carried to the Isles of the Blessed. Its appearance here, in a passage that looks back on the war from a later time, fits that perspective: the narrator speaks of the heroes as a race that has ended. Compare the repeated phrase 'such as mortals now are' (12.383, 12.449), measuring the heroes against the weaker men of the present.

title: The rivers of Mount Ida
greek: Ῥῆσός θ᾽ Ἑπτάπορός τε Κάρησός τε Ῥοδίος τε / Γρήνικός τε καὶ Αἴσηπος (Rhēsos, Heptaporos, Karēsos, Rhodios, Grēnikos, Aisēpos)
short: Eight rivers flowing from Mount Ida are turned against the wall; most appear only here, but the Granicus later became famous for Alexander's victory.
body: The list of rivers is a small catalogue. Leaf notes that all of them except the Caresus appear in Hesiod's list of the river-children of Ocean and Tethys (Theogony 337-45), so the two poets share a traditional inventory of the rivers of the Troad. Only the Aesepus, Scamander and Simois appear elsewhere in Homer. The Granicus is famous in later history as the site of Alexander the Great's first victory over the Persians (334 BC); the rest are otherwise unknown. The Simois is the river 'by whose banks many shields of bull's-hide and helms fell in the dust'; Leaf compares Virgil's echo, where Aeneas recalls the Simois rolling the shields, helmets and bodies of the brave (Aeneid 1.100-1). Apollo turns all their mouths together for nine days and Zeus rains continually, an image of a deluge that some scholars connect with flood stories.

title: Polydamas, Hector's prudent adviser
greek: Πουλυδάμας (Poulydamas)
short: Polydamas, Hector's companion, gives cautious advice; in Book 12 Hector first accepts it and then angrily rejects it, a pattern that ends in disaster.
body: Polydamas is the son of Panthous and, we later learn, was born on the same night as Hector (18.251-2). He plays the role of wise counsellor to Hector four times: here at 12.60-79, where Hector accepts his plan to leave the chariots at the trench; at 12.210-29, after the eagle omen, where Hector rejects him; at 13.726-47; and at 18.254-83, where he urges retreat into the city and Hector overrules him, a mistake Hector admits before his death (22.99-103). Leaf notes the inconsistency between the two scenes of Book 12: Polydamas begins his second speech complaining that Hector always rebukes him, although Hector has just taken his advice. Leaf suspects that Polydamas first belonged to the Book 18 scene and was added here later. For readers, the pattern matters more than its origin: Polydamas is the voice of prudence, and Hector's growing deafness to him tracks his overconfidence in Zeus' promise.

title: Asius and the narrator's 'fool!' (nēpios)
greek: νήπιος (nēpios)
short: Asius refuses to leave his chariot and drives at the gate; the narrator calls him 'fool' (nēpios), foreseeing that he will never return to Ilios.
body: Nēpios literally means 'infant, without understanding'. When the narrator applies it to a character, he speaks from his superior knowledge of what is to come: the character acts in ignorance of his fate. Patroclus receives the same word at 16.46 as he begs for the armour that will lead to his death, and Andromache at 22.445 as she prepares a bath for Hector who is already dead. Asius, son of Hyrtacus from Arisbe, disobeys Polydamas' counsel and drives his chariot to the left-hand gate; he dies at Idomeneus' hands in Book 13 (13.384-93). Leaf thinks the whole Asius episode was added to explain why Asius is found with his chariot among the ships in Book 13, and notes that it leads to nothing and is simply left without an ending. Its narrative function is nevertheless clear: Asius' failure contrasts with Sarpedon's and Hector's assaults, and the narrator's 'fool!' lends it a tragic irony.

title: The Lapiths Polypoetes and Leonteus
greek: Λαπίθαι (Lapithai); ὡς ὅτε τε δρύες οὔρεσιν ὑψικάρηνοι (hōs hote te drues ouresin hypsikarēnoi)
short: Two Lapith warriors hold the gate against Asius, standing firm like mountain oaks and then charging like wild boars.
body: The Lapiths were a Thessalian people famous for their battle with the Centaurs at the wedding of Peirithous, which Nestor recalls at 1.262-8. Polypoetes is Peirithous' son. Outside this episode the Lapiths are not named in the Iliad, as Monro notes, though both leaders appear in the Catalogue (2.738-47). The pair receive two similes in quick succession. First they stand before the gate like oaks with deep roots that endure wind and rain day after day; then they rush out like wild boars that break the trees around them, so that the bronze clatters on their breasts as the boars' tusks clatter. Leaf objects that the second picture contradicts the first; others see a deliberate shift from passive endurance to counterattack. The Centaur battle would later become one of the great subjects of Greek temple sculpture (Olympia, the Parthenon metopes), as a symbol of civilisation against savagery.

title: Asius accuses Zeus: 'a lover of lies'
greek: Ζεῦ πάτερ, ἦ ῥά νυ καὶ σὺ φιλοψευδὴς ἐτέτυξο (Zeu pater, ē rha ny kai sy philopseudēs etetuxo)
short: Frustrated at the gate, Asius strikes his thighs and calls Zeus 'utterly a lover of lies', because he had believed Zeus would give the Trojans an easy victory.
body: Philopseudēs, 'lie-loving', occurs only here in Homer. Homeric heroes regularly reproach the gods when they feel deceived: Menelaus calls Zeus 'the most destructive of gods' when his sword shatters (3.365), and Agamemnon complains of Zeus' 'evil deceit' (2.114, 9.21). Striking the thighs is a conventional gesture of anguish or frustration. Asius' complaint is wrong about the facts, since Zeus never promised him anything; the promise of glory was given to Hector (11.186-94), and the narrator confirms at once that Zeus 'willed to vouchsafe glory' to Hector, not to Asius. Yet the speech voices a real theme of the Iliad: men cannot see the will of Zeus whole, and his plan works through deceptions, such as the false Dream sent to Agamemnon in Book 2. The god of the poem is not a guarantor of fairness to individual fighters.

title: The wasps and bees simile
greek: σφῆκες μέσον αἰόλοι (sphēkes meson aioloi)
short: Asius compares the two Lapiths to wasps or bees that will not leave their nest on a rocky path but fight off hunters to protect their young.
body: The simile is unusual in being spoken by a character rather than the narrator. Aiolos, here 'nimble', is debated: Monro, following Buttmann, takes it in its original sense of quick-moving, while Leaf prefers 'bright-coloured, variegated' and lists both views; in Homer the word is also used of glancing armour and of a writhing snake (12.208). Wasps and bees appear elsewhere as images of massed, angry defenders (the Myrmidons at 16.259-65 swarm out like wasps disturbed by boys; the Greeks muster like bees at 2.87-90). Leaf points out a difficulty: the image of a swarm suits a whole army better than two men, and Erhardt proposed a small change that would refer it to all the Greeks. The final line, that they will not give way 'till they either slay or be slain', restates the heroic choice Odysseus formulated at 11.410.

anchor: as though I were a god
title: The narrator's voice: 'hard for me, as if I were a god, to tell all this'
greek: ἀργαλέον δέ με ταῦτα θεὸν ὣς πάντ᾽ ἀγορεῦσαι (argaleon de me tauta theon hōs pant' agoreusai)
short: The narrator steps forward in the first person: to tell everything happening at every gate would need a god's knowledge.
body: The Homeric narrator very rarely says 'I'. The closest parallels are the invocation before the Catalogue, where he says that he could not name the multitude even with ten tongues unless the Muses helped (2.484-93), and the apostrophes to Patroclus and Menelaus. Here he admits a limit: the battle rages at many gates at once, and only a god could report it all. The ancient critics rejected lines 175-80, and Monro thinks them probably spurious, since they anticipate fighting at other gates that is never described. Leaf observes that the introduction of the poet's personality is a mark of late origin, that 'the wall of stone' is awkwardly phrased, and that the mention of fire is premature, as the Trojans have not yet reached the ships. Whatever their origin, the lines show the narrator's sense that his story is selective, that he follows one thread of a battle too large to tell whole.

title: The omen of the eagle and the snake
greek: αἰετὸς ὑψιπέτης ... φοινήεντα δράκοντα (aietos hypsipetēs ... phoinēenta drakonta); Διὸς τέρας αἰγιόχοιο (Dios teras aigiochoio)
short: As the Trojans prepare to cross the trench, an eagle flying on their left drops a wounded snake among them; Polydamas reads it as a warning.
body: The eagle is Zeus' bird, and the narrator calls the sign 'a portent of Zeus who bears the aegis'. It seizes a blood-red snake, but the snake, still alive, bites its breast, and the eagle drops it among the Trojans and flies off screaming. Polydamas interprets it as a soothsayer would (12.217-29): like the eagle, the Trojans will reach the Greek ships but fail to carry off their prize, and return in disorder with heavy losses. His reading proves broadly correct, since the Trojans will be driven back in Books 15-16, though only after much success. The image of the eagle and the snake had a long afterlife: it is imitated by Virgil (Aeneid 11.751-6) and becomes a stock emblem of conflict. Leaf discusses the textual difficulties of lines 203-4 (who bites whom), and observes that the eagle passes 'on the left', which matters for the augury that follows.

anchor: whether they fare to the right
title: Augury: birds on the right and the left
greek: οἰωνοῖσι τανυπτερύγεσσι (oiōnoisi tanypterygessi); εἴτ᾽ ἐπὶ δεξί᾽ ἴωσι ... εἴτ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἀριστερά (eit' epi dexi' iōsi ... eit' ep' aristera)
short: Hector scorns the 'long-winged birds', whether they fly to the right toward the dawn and the sun, or to the left toward the misty dark.
body: Greek bird-divination (oiōnoskopia) treated birds on the right, or flying from left to right, as lucky, and those on the left as unlucky. Monro concludes from this passage that the observer faced north, so that the east (dawn) lay on the right. Leaf discusses the question at length and cites H. D. Darbishire's argument that 'dawn' and 'darkness' in Hector's line may mean south and north rather than east and west; if so, the augur would normally have faced east, and the old inference that he faced north falls away. His general conclusion is useful: in Homer omens encourage or discourage a decision already taken, but never determine it, so that Hector's indifference is 'in the spirit of the Homeric age'. That is why a professional seer is needed, someone who 'knew omens clearly' (12.229), the kind of interpreter Polydamas invokes at 12.228-9.

title: 'One omen is best: to fight for one's country'
greek: εἷς οἰωνὸς ἄριστος, ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης (heis oiōnos aristos, amynesthai peri patrēs)
short: Hector's famous reply to Polydamas: the only omen that matters is to defend one's homeland. Aristotle quotes it as a model maxim.
body: Hector rejects the bird-sign in favour of Zeus' direct promise (11.186-94), and sums up his position in a single line that became proverbial. Aristotle cites it in the Rhetoric (2.21) as an example of a maxim (gnōmē) used against received opinion. Leaf counts Hector's 'outburst' to Polydamas among the two finest passages of the book. Hector's words express a real heroic value, and he is the Iliad's great defender of his city, wife and child; but the context makes the line double-edged. He is wrong about this omen, and his scorn for Polydamas, whom he threatens to kill if he holds back (12.248-50), shows the confidence that will destroy him. The same pattern recurs in Book 18, when Hector rejects Polydamas' advice to retreat behind the walls, and in Book 22, when he recognises that his 'recklessness' (atasthaliai) has ruined his people (22.104).

anchor: as flakes of snow fall thick
title: The great snow simile
greek: ὥς τε νιφάδες χιόνος πίπτωσι θαμειαί (hōs te niphades chionos piptōsi thameiai); κῆλα (kēla), shafts
short: Stones fly as thick as snowflakes on a windless winter day, when Zeus shows men 'these arrows of his' and buries all the land but the shore.
body: This is one of the most elaborate similes in Homer. Zeus 'bestirs himself to snow', lulls the winds, and blankets mountain peaks, headlands, grassy plains and farmland; only the waves at the shore keep it off. Leaf notes that the same comparison was used more briefly a little earlier (12.156-8). The snowflakes are Zeus' kēla, a word used only of divine missiles, as Hesiod uses it of Zeus' thunder and lightning (Theogony 707-8); Leaf compares Job 38.22-3, where God keeps 'the treasures of the snow' for 'the day of battle and war'. The simile's stillness and silence contrast with the din of the battle it illustrates, and its total covering of the world suggests the impartial, overwhelming force of the war. Leaf's introduction calls the similes of this book 'on the whole the most elaborate and beautiful in Homer'.

title: Sarpedon as a hungry mountain lion
greek: λέων ὀρεσίτροφος (leōn oresitrophos)
short: Zeus rouses his son Sarpedon against the wall, and he advances like a starving lion that will attack a guarded fold even if he dies in the attempt.
body: Sarpedon, son of Zeus and leader of the Lycians, Troy's most important allies, now becomes the focus of the assault. The narrator first describes his shield (beaten bronze stitched over many layers of bull's-hide with gold wire) and then compares him to a mountain lion long without meat. Its spirit drives it into the close-built fold even though the herdsmen keep watch with dogs and spears: either it seizes a sheep or is itself struck by a javelin. The simile prepares exactly the choice Sarpedon will put into words to Glaucus a few lines later, to win glory or give it to another. Lion similes are the commonest in the Iliad and usually mark a hero at his most aggressive; this one, with its stress on hunger and the risk of death, gives the lion's courage a tragic edge. Leaf suggests that this attack and Hector's were originally parallel versions of the breaching of the wall.

anchor: seats, and messes, and full cups
title: Sarpedon's speech (1): honour brings obligation
greek: ἕδρῃ τε κρέασίν τε ἰδὲ πλείοις δεπάεσσιν (hedrēi te kreasin te ide pleiois depaessin); τέμενος (temenos)
short: Sarpedon reminds Glaucus that they enjoy the best seats, meat, wine and land in Lycia; they must earn these privileges by fighting in the front line.
body: This speech is often read as the clearest statement of the heroic code in Homer. Sarpedon lists the material marks of honour (timē): the seat of honour, the best portions of meat and full cups at feasts (compare 8.161-2, where Hector mocks Diomedes for losing these), and a temenos, an estate 'cut off' from common land, by the river Xanthus, with orchards and wheat-fields; Lycian kings had given such a temenos to Bellerophon (6.194-5), as Monro and Leaf note. The logic is reciprocal. The community grants these honours, and the leaders justify them by fighting among the foremost, so that the Lycians may say 'no inglorious men are these that rule in Lycia'. The privileges are not simply enjoyed; they are a debt to be repaid in danger. Compare Peleus' charge to Achilles to be 'always best' (11.784).

title: Sarpedon's speech (2): why mortals must seek glory
greek: εἰ μὲν γὰρ πόλεμον περὶ τόνδε φυγόντε / αἰεὶ δὴ μέλλοιμεν ἀγήρω τ᾽ ἀθανάτω τε (ei men gar polemon peri tonde phygonte aiei dē melloimen agērō t' athanatō te)
short: If they could escape death by avoiding battle, Sarpedon says, he would not fight; but death comes anyway, so let them win glory or give it to another.
body: The second half of the speech grounds the heroic code in mortality. If the two of them could escape this war and live 'ageless and immortal' for ever, Sarpedon would not fight in the front line or send Glaucus there; but since 'fates of death' (kēres thanatoio) stand around us in thousands, which no mortal can escape, let us go forward, 'whether we give glory to another, or another to us'. Glory (kleos) is the only answer to death, since only fame outlives the body. Leaf calls the passage noble and 'almost elegiac', and quotes Robert Wood's anecdote of Lord Granville, who on his deathbed in 1763 recited these lines in Greek, dwelling on 12.324, before discussing the Treaty of Paris. The speech is given extra weight by Sarpedon's own fate: Zeus will consider saving him in Book 16 and decide that he must die (16.431-61).

title: Epicles falls 'like a diver'
greek: ἀρνευτῆρι ἐοικώς (arneutēri eoikōs)
short: Aias crushes Epicles' helmet with a huge stone, and he falls from the high wall like a diver plunging headfirst.
body: The stone is described as one that a man 'such as mortals now are' could hardly lift with both hands, a recurrent measure of the heroes' greater strength (5.304, 12.449, 20.287). Epicles falls 'like a diver' (arneutēr). Monro explains the word from arneuō, 'to take a header', from the likeness of the action to a ram (arnos, 'lamb') butting. The comparison is brief but grimly vivid; the same word describes Cebriones falling from his chariot at 16.742, and Patroclus mocks him with a long sarcastic speech about his skill as a diver for oysters (16.745-50). Teucer, Aias' half-brother and the best Greek archer, then wounds Glaucus, who withdraws secretly so that no Greek can boast over him. Homeric battle is full of such small, exactly observed deaths, each given a moment of individual attention.

title: Zeus saves his son Sarpedon, for now
greek: ἀλλὰ Ζεὺς κῆρας ἄμυνε / παιδὸς ἑοῦ (alla Zeus kēras amyne paidos heou)
short: Teucer's arrow strikes Sarpedon's baldric, but Zeus keeps the fates of death from his son, so that he does not die at the ships' sterns.
body: The line implies that Sarpedon's death is only postponed. Zeus 'wards off the fates' here because it is not yet the place or time: Sarpedon is fated to die at Patroclus' hands in the plain (16.419-507). In Book 16 Zeus will ask Hera whether he should snatch his son from death, and she will warn him that the other gods will not approve if he overrides fate; he yields, and sheds bloody raindrops in his honour (16.459-61). The present rescue thus creates expectation. Meanwhile Sarpedon makes the first real breach: he grips the battlement, tears it away and opens a path for many. Leaf notes that an earlier version may have had Sarpedon actually first to break in, since at 16.558 he is called the man 'who first leapt within the wall of the Achaeans', a phrase this book gives to Hector (12.438).

title: Two men disputing the boundary-stones
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὥ τ᾽ ἀμφ᾽ οὔροισι δύ᾽ ἀνέρε δηριάασθον / μέτρ᾽ ἐν χερσὶν ἔχοντες ἐπιξύνῳ ἐν ἀρούρῃ (hōs d' hō t' amph' ouroisi dy' anere dēriaasthon metr' en chersin echontes epixynōi en aroururēi)
short: Lycians and Greeks contend across the battlement like two neighbours with measuring-rods quarrelling over boundary-stones in a shared field.
body: The neighbours stand in a narrow strip of a 'common field' (epixynos aroura), each claiming his equal share. Leaf and Monro take the simile as evidence for an open-field system in which the community's land was divided into strips marked by movable stones (oura); such stones could be shifted by a dishonest neighbour, and only remeasurement could settle the quarrel. Athena later uses a boundary-stone as a weapon (21.403-5). The comparison catches the stalemate exactly: neither side can push the other off the wall, and each fights over a few feet of ground. It is also typical of the Iliad's practice of comparing war to the ordinary disputes and labours of peace, which reminds the audience how small and human the stakes of the fighting are, even at its most terrible.

title: The wool-weighing woman: a balance held even
greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἔχον ὥς τε τάλαντα γυνὴ χερνῆτις ἀληθής (all' echon hōs te talanta gynē chernētis alēthēs)
short: The battle stays balanced like the scales of a working woman weighing wool, careful to make them exactly even so she can earn a meagre wage for her children.
body: Chernētis means a woman who works for hire with her hands, a day-labourer. Leaf calls the simile 'particularly interesting' as one of our few glimpses into the life of the Homeric poor: elsewhere wool-working is done by the women of a household for themselves, even by queens, but here spinning is apparently put out for pay. He takes alēthēs in its old sense of 'not forgetting', careful, anxious about her task, rather than 'honest', and stresses that her wage is meagre and probably paid in kind. The scales recall the golden scales in which Zeus weighs the fates of the two armies (8.69-74) and of Hector and Achilles (22.209-13). The pathos of the simile is unusual: a poor mother's livelihood depends on an exact balance, as the lives of the fighters do. The balance tips at once: Zeus gives Hector the glory, and he is first to leap within the wall.

title: Hector lifts the stone like a shepherd's fleece
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε ποιμὴν ῥεῖα φέρει πόκον ἄρσενος οἰός (hōs d' hote poimēn rheia pherei pokon arsenos oios)
short: Hector carries a stone two of the strongest men now living could not lift, as easily as a shepherd carries a ram's fleece, because Zeus makes it light.
body: The stone lies before the gate, broad at the base and pointed at the top; 'not easily might two men, the mightiest of the folk, such as mortals now are' have heaved it onto a wagon. Zeus, 'son of crooked-counselling Cronos', makes it light for Hector. Ancient critics rejected line 450 as diminishing the hero's feat, but Leaf, following Heyne, answers that divine aid explains a hero's superiority without lessening it: in Homer the gods work through human strength. The shepherd simile, carrying a fleece in one hand, makes the weight vanish. Leaf also cites Hehn's observation that pokos means wool plucked out, and that shearing may not yet have been known. Hector plants his feet apart, hurls the stone, and smashes both hinges of the double gate. The image of effortlessness is a sign of how fully Zeus is with Hector at this moment.

title: Hector breaks the gate: 'his face like sudden night'
greek: νυκτὶ θοῇ ἀτάλαντος ὑπώπια (nykti thoēi atalantos hypōpia)
short: Hector leaps through the shattered gate, his face like swift-falling night and his eyes blazing with fire; the Greeks flee to their ships.
body: This is the climax of the 'Battle at the Wall' (teichomachia) that gives the book its ancient title. Hector's face is 'equal to swift night', recalling Apollo, who came down from Olympus 'like the night' (1.47); Leaf notes that hypōpia here means the face in general, and that one might expect the darkness to be above the eyes, in the brow. No one could have stopped him 'save the gods', the eyes blaze with fire, and the Trojans pour over the wall and through the gate. The book ends on the Greeks driven in rout among the hollow ships and an unceasing din. The breaching of the wall fulfils the stage of Zeus' plan announced to Hector at 11.186-94 and brings the Trojans to the ships, where the battle will remain until Patroclus intervenes in Book 16. The wall, built in Book 7 and destined to vanish (12.3-35), has lasted barely a day of fighting.
